Medium · Finance and payments

Checkout payments

Online shops send you their customers at the moment they pay. You call a card processor, record the order and answer in a couple of seconds. When the processor is slow or down, shoppers refresh and tap Pay again. Practise this medium system design problem for free with a Google or GitHub account.

Play this problem

The brief

Online shops send you their customers at the moment they pay. You call a card processor, record the order and answer in a couple of seconds. When the processor is slow or down, shoppers refresh and tap Pay again.

Think of a checkout like Stripe Checkout.

Users, scale and requirements

Who uses it
8 million shoppers a month
Audience in plain numbers
8,000,000 people per month
Normal peak
≈ 2,000 requests per second
Request mix
Read: 50%; Write: 15%; Payment: 20%; Sign-in: 15%
Speed for 99 of 100 requests
Read: ≈ 300 ms; Write: ≈ 300 ms; Payment: ≈ 3,500 ms; Sign-in: ≈ 1,000 ms
Successful requests
99.9%
Data safety
No acknowledged write may be lost.
Monthly budget
≈ $5,200
Data at rest
≈ 2 TB
Where users are
North America: 70%; Europe: 30%
Home region
North America
Waiting deadlines
Read: 900 seconds; Write: 3,600 seconds; Payment: 3,600 seconds; Sign-in: 900 seconds
Personal reads
80% of reads are private; a shared public copy cannot answer them.
Required proofs
Managed encryption keys; Audit trail

≈ marks an approximation, just as in the game. Waiting deadlines measure the age of queued work and are separate from interactive response time.

  • The processor itself is paid from revenue and is not in this budget.
  • Peak is early evening.

Questions that shape the design

What happens if the shopper taps Pay twice?

They must be charged once. Every attempt carries a unique key from the browser.

If the processor is down, should checkout fail?

Better to say "payment pending" and settle after than to lose the sale, as long as nobody is charged twice.

Is card data sensitive?

Yes. Payments need an audit trail and keys held in a key service.

How slow is the processor?

About 0.4 s typically and 2 s at the slow end. It accepts about 1,000 charges a second for you.

The traffic day

Consumer traffic, busiest in the evening. The clock covers 00:00 to 24:00 in the home region. Events add pressure on top of that normal traffic.

  1. 10:30 · Duplicate delivery

    The queue redelivers messages. Without duplicate protection, side effects may be applied twice.

    Affected share: 1%. Duration: ≈ 3,600 seconds.

  2. 13:00 · Slow dependency

    An outside service slows down. Your servers fill with requests waiting on it.

    Added response time: ≈ 3,000 ms. Duration: ≈ 1,800 seconds.

  3. 19:30 · Dependency outage

    An outside service fails calls during an outage.

    Failed calls: 100%. Duration: ≈ 1,200 seconds.

What a strong design has to handle

  • When the processor is slow, your servers wait on it and run out of room for everyone else. How do you stop waiting?
  • Resolve unknown charges and keep order state consistent with payment state.
  • Synchronous is simpler and gives instant "paid" or "declined". Its weak spot is a full outage: while the processor is down, nobody can pay.
  • Asynchronous survives an outage and smooths bursts, but the shopper has to accept "pending", and your support team has to explain it.

Make a prediction, run a full traffic day, then compare the result. The in-game editorial opens after a finished day and includes measured reference designs.

Concepts to practise

  • Exactly once, on purpose
  • Timeouts and failing fast
  • Work across services
  • What consistent really means

Related problems

  • Medium

    Buy now, pay later

    At checkout a shopper picks "pay in four". You score the shopper in a few seconds, then charge the first quarter on their card. The card network sometimes asks you to slow down, and when apps retry, the retries make it worse.

  • Medium

    Notification service

    Every other team asks you to send messages: order shipped, new login, a sale starting. You send them by push, email and text through outside providers who have their own limits. Send each message once, and never block the team that asked.

  • Hard

    Scheduled job service

    Customers register jobs: "call my web address every night at 02:00" or "every hour on the hour". Aim to fire within 5 seconds; work still waiting after 60 seconds counts as failed. Retry safely after a crash. One external effect requires the customer endpoint to honor a stable job occurrence key. Half the world picks the top of the hour, so a huge crowd of jobs comes due in the same second.

  • Medium

    One-to-one chat

    People send short messages to each other from their phones. A message must arrive once, in order, even when the phone is on a bad connection and sends it again. If the other person is offline, the message waits and a notification goes out.
